Barrier Blue Pontiac Bonneville Convertible Looks Better at 60 Than It Did Back in 1966
22 photos
Photo: Vanguard Motor Sales
This 1966 Pontiac Bonneville Convertible has recently walked out of the restoration shop, rocking head-turning blue paint over a blue interior and V8 firepower. Never a garage queen, the car has over 94,000 miles on the clock and is longing to be driven.
Finished in what Pontiac called Barrier Blue Metallic and sporting a white power-operated convertible top over a Morrokide interior, this 1966 Pontiac Bonneville probably looks better than it did the day it rolled off the production line of the Pontiac Assembly Plant in Michigan. In the meantime, many of its siblings rot in barns or junkyards, begging for restoration .
General Motors built 135,331 Bonnevilles in 1966, with the rarest body style (only 3,000 units built) being the four-door six-seat station wagon. Meanwhile, the two-door convertible, like this car right here, came second, with 16,229 examples, accounting for 12% of all Bonnevilles built that year.
The Pontiac Bonneville was built on General Motors' full-sized B-body platform and sat on a stretched, exclusive 124-inch (3,150-millimeter) wheelbase that was 3 inches (76.2 millimeters) longer than that of the entry-level Pontiac Catalina.
Photo: Vanguard Motor Sales The open-top variant came with the rakish fender lines, heavy ribbed lower-body chrome trim, and sleek rear fender skirts that elongated the vehicle visually. In the meantime, the cabin put on a premium show. A real wood-veneered instrument panel was integrated directly into the dashboard.
Pontiac also offered a tilt steering column, a remote mirror control, an automatic vacuum-operated trunk release, and the Wonder Touch power steering. To enhance the premium label, the power-operated convertible top featured a tempered glass rear window rather than the usual plastic.
The Bonneville convertible is set in motion by the 389 cubic-inch (6.4-liter) V8, with distinct factory ratings, depending on the transmission. This car comes with the Turbo Hydra-matic automatic transmission, which means the V8 pushes out 325 horsepower (330 metric horsepower) and 429 pound-feet (582 Newton meters) of torque.
This exact same engine, but with the factory Tri-Power option and dialed up to produce 360 horsepower (365 metric horsepower), was under the hood of the Pontiac GTO, the absolute pioneer of the American muscle car era, debuting on October 1, 1963.
Photo: Vanguard Motor Sales However, for the Bonneville, it was enough to make the convertible accelerate from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 8.4 seconds (the four-speed manual was over a second quicker) and max out at 119 mph (192 kph). Power brakes and power steering are also on the menu.
The Pontiac Bonneville, which has recently been through a frame-off restoration, is equipped with air conditioning. The ultra-thin, two-spoke steering wheel frames a speedometer scaled up to 120 mph (193 kph) and an odometer indicating 94,313 miles (151,782 kilometers). It may not sound like much of a globetrotter considering that the car saw the light of day 60 years ago. However, it shows that it is no garage queen.
Now, this no-garage-queen is in search of a new home and an owner who will drive it until its wheels fall off. Vanguard Motors listed it with a price of $119,900. That is far above the average. classic.com indicates that impeccably restored Bonnevilles reaching concours level can go well beyond the $60,000 on the collector car market. But this one right here sits well above the standard market average
Back in 1966, customers who wanted to go home with a Pontiac Bonneville Convertible had to pay a starting price of $3,586. Adjusted for inflation, that would be roughly $35,600. That is Toyota Camry Hybrid money.
